title: English Vocabulary 1 · Units 33–34
description: Editorial review of Units 33–34: UK culture and crime, covering source illustrations, teaching tables, exercises, usage patterns, British English IPA, Portuguese translations and original examples. Human sign-off and real application testing remain outstanding.
sourceNotice: Learning targets were checked against the user-supplied textbook, printed pages 72–75 (PDF pages 73–76). Example sentences and explanatory notes are original; textbook images, exercises and extended passages are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Reviewed teaching pages and illustrations, special-days and school tables, crimes/criminals/verbs table, common mistakes, food, politics, law, and exercises 33.1–33.5 and 34.1–34.4. Original unit and item IDs are retained.
audit.pronunciation: British English phonemic transcriptions checked against the source British English index when indexed; unindexed inflected forms and longer phrases were reviewed compositionally. Native-speaker and TTS playback checks remain pending.
audit.cannotGuarantee: The inspected content covers principal teaching and exercise targets, not verbatim copies of exercises or a guarantee of every contextual inference. Real VocabLab browser import, speech synthesis, study-progress migration, and backup/restore were not tested.

editorialReview.reviewMethod: Inspected the illustrated teaching pages, exercise prompts and tables of both units; reviewed every original item, translated metadata, notes and objectives into English, verified British IPA against the textbook index where applicable and validated JSON structure and IDs locally.
editorialReview.notes: Human editorial approval, actual VocabLab importer testing, real TTS playback and stored study-progress/backup checks remain necessary before release approval. The original package, unit and item IDs are preserved.

units.title: Unit 33 — UK culture
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 33. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.

items.example: Our town has a music festival every summer.
items.note: A broad label for public celebrations. The unit groups traditional festivals and special days with associated customs.

items.example: We usually visit our grandparents at Christmas.
items.note: The textbook gives 25 December as Christmas Day. Use at Christmas to refer to the holiday period.

items.example: I found a Christmas card from my aunt.
items.note: A card sent at Christmas. A useful collocation is send Christmas cards.

items.example: My family sends Christmas cards to old friends.
items.note: Send – sent – sent is irregular. Sending cards is among the Christmas customs listed in the source.

items.example: I bought a small present for my sister.
items.note: The noun has initial stress, /ˈprezənt/; the verb present has final stress, /prɪˈzent/.

items.example: We give presents to the children on Christmas morning.
items.note: Give – gave – given is irregular. You can give someone a present or give a present to someone.

items.example: I want to spend more time with my family this winter.
items.note: Spend – spent – spent is irregular. Say spend time with someone, not spend time to someone.

items.example: There is a tall Christmas tree in the living room.
items.note: A compound noun for a decorated tree associated with Christmas. Compare decorate a Christmas tree.

items.example: The children helped us decorate a Christmas tree.
items.note: Decorate takes a direct object: decorate a tree, not decorate to a tree.

items.example: We had dinner together on New Year’s Eve.
items.note: Eve means the day or evening before an event. New Year’s Eve is on 31 December; use on with the day.

items.example: My friends celebrated Hogmanay in Edinburgh.
items.note: The Scottish name for New Year’s Eve celebrations. Hogmanay is especially associated with Scotland.

items.example: Everyone began to sing and dance after dinner.
items.note: The festival table associates these activities with New Year’s Eve. The past tense of sing is sang.

items.example: At midnight, we toasted the New Year together.
items.note: Here toast is a verb meaning celebrate with a drink; it is also a noun meaning bread or a ceremonial drink.

items.example: The office is closed on New Year’s Day.
items.note: New Year’s Day is on 1 January, one day after New Year’s Eve.

items.example: Most offices are closed because it is a bank holiday.
items.note: A public holiday in the UK, not simply a day on which banks close. Many workplaces may be closed.

items.pt: Dia de São Valentim; Dia dos Namorados (14 de fevereiro, no Reino Unido)
items.example: She wrote a lovely card for Valentine’s Day.
items.note: The UK date is 14 February. This is different from the date used for the corresponding Brazilian celebration.

items.pt: enviar um cartão de Dia dos Namorados
items.example: He sent a Valentine’s Day card to his partner.
items.note: The preposition to identifies the recipient: send a card to someone. The phrase makes the Valentine’s Day context explicit.

items.example: Her boyfriend lives in another city.
items.note: The source lists a boyfriend as someone who might receive a Valentine’s Day card.

items.example: His girlfriend loves receiving letters.
items.note: The source lists a girlfriend as someone who might receive a Valentine’s Day card.

items.example: We are going to visit our cousins at Easter.
items.note: The date of Easter changes from year to year. Use at Easter for the holiday period.

items.example: She gave her nephew a chocolate Easter egg.
items.note: The source means a chocolate egg given at Easter, not an ordinary egg served as food.

items.pt: dar ovos de Páscoa às crianças
items.example: They give children Easter eggs every spring.
items.note: Give someone something: give children Easter eggs. Children is the irregular plural of child.

items.example: The children wore costumes for Halloween.
items.note: Halloween is on 31 October. The textbook associates it with dressing up and asking for sweets.

items.example: The children dressed up for the school party.
items.note: To dress up for Halloween usually means to wear a costume; dress up can also mean to wear smart clothes.

items.example: I heard someone knock at the door.
items.note: Both knock at the door and knock on the door are natural. Do not use knock the door for this meaning.

items.example: The children knocked at our door to ask for sweets.
items.note: Ask for introduces what somebody wants. The source links this expression with children at Halloween.

items.example: She bought some sweets for the party.
items.note: British English sweets are commonly called candy in American English.

items.example: We watched the fireworks on Bonfire Night.
items.note: Bonfire Night is observed on 5 November and is associated with bonfires and fireworks.

items.example: A large bonfire burned in the field.
items.note: A large outdoor fire. A bonfire is different from a display of fireworks.

items.pt: fazer uma fogueira; reunir-se ao redor de uma fogueira
items.example: The village will have a bonfire on Saturday.
items.note: A natural collocation in the textbook’s Bonfire Night description: have a bonfire.

items.example: The fireworks lit up the night sky.
items.note: Often plural when referring to a display. You can watch fireworks or set off fireworks.

items.example: The dates vary from year to year.
items.note: The source says that Easter dates vary; vary is a regular verb meaning change or differ.

items.example: They serve traditional food in that café.
items.note: An adjective modifying a noun, as in traditional food. The source presents familiar UK dishes.

items.example: We shared some fish and chips by the sea.
items.note: This fixed expression names a well-known meal, not simply two unrelated foods.

items.example: We ate roast beef on Sunday.
items.note: Roast describes beef cooked in an oven. Beef refers to meat from cattle.

items.example: My father made roast potatoes for lunch.
items.note: Potatoes cooked by roasting in an oven. Contrast roast potatoes with fried chips.

items.example: We roast vegetables in the oven.
items.note: In this unit, roast can describe food cooked in an oven or mean cook in an oven.

items.example: Put the potatoes in the oven for half an hour.
items.note: Food is cooked in the oven, not on the oven, when the intended meaning is inside the appliance.

items.example: Yorkshire pudding is often served with roast beef.
items.note: Despite the word pudding, this is a savoury baked accompaniment often served with roast meat, not a sweet dessert.

items.example: We need more flour for this recipe.
items.note: Usually uncountable when referring to the ingredient. The source lists flour, milk and eggs in Yorkshire pudding.

items.pt: frango tikka masala (prato com molho temperado)
items.example: She ordered chicken tikka masala at the restaurant.
items.note: The source describes it as a kind of curry popular in the UK and gives India as its origin; detailed culinary origins are debated.

items.pt: curry; prato com molho e especiarias
items.example: We had a mild vegetable curry for dinner.
items.note: The source uses a kind of curry to explain chicken tikka masala.

items.example: Their three-year-old daughter goes to nursery school.
items.note: The textbook gives ages 2–4 as a simplified guide, not a universal admission rule.

items.example: He started primary school this year.
items.note: The textbook gives ages 5–11 as a broad example; actual arrangements can vary across the UK.

items.pt: escola secundária; ensino posterior ao primário
items.example: Her brother is still at secondary school.
items.note: The textbook gives ages 12–18 as a simplified range; school stages vary by nation and institution.

items.example: Both children attend a state school.
items.note: In UK usage, a state school is publicly funded and does not charge ordinary tuition fees to parents.

items.example: They decided to send their daughter to a private school.
items.note: In this textbook a private school is a fee-paying school. UK public school is a different term from American public school.

items.pt: pagar pela escola; pagar pelos estudos
items.example: Some parents pay for school, while others do not.
items.note: Use pay for with a service. The source contrasts schools where parents pay with those where they do not.

items.pt: ir à escola; frequentar a escola
items.example: The children go to school near their home.
items.note: Use go to school without an article when referring to attending school as an institution.

items.example: My colleague moved to the UK last year.
items.note: The UK means the United Kingdom, comprising England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland; the article the is normally used.

items.example: The royal family attended an official ceremony.
items.note: The royal family belongs to the monarchy and should not be confused with the elected government.

items.example: The king gave a short speech.
items.note: The male monarch is a king. The source discusses a king or a queen without identifying a current individual.

items.example: The queen met visitors at the palace.
items.note: The female monarch is a queen. This is not the same political office as Prime Minister.

items.example: Tourists visited the Houses of Parliament in London.
items.note: The Houses of Parliament in London are associated with the UK Parliament, not the home of the royal family.

items.example: Important political decisions were discussed yesterday.
items.note: Make a decision is the usual collocation. The textbook associates political decisions with Parliament.

items.example: The Prime Minister answered questions in Parliament.
items.note: The Prime Minister leads the UK government; the officeholder can change, so no current name is supplied.

items.example: A political leader spoke to the journalists.
items.note: The source uses political leader to describe the Prime Minister; the title is not interchangeable with monarch.

learningObjectives: Recognise British festivals and their dates and describe customs using send cards, dress up, give presents, and toast the New Year.
Distinguish New Year’s Eve from New Year’s Day and understand Hogmanay and the British term bank holiday.
Identify the dishes in the source, including fish and chips, roast beef, roast potatoes, Yorkshire pudding and chicken tikka masala.
Recognise that Yorkshire pudding is a savoury food often eaten with a roast rather than a sweet dessert.
Distinguish nursery, primary, secondary, state and private schools using the simplified ages and payment categories presented in the source.
Understand the roles of the royal family, king or queen, Houses of Parliament and Prime Minister without confusing monarchy with elected government.
Use natural collocations for celebrations and recognise that questions about current political officeholders require up-to-date information.

units.title: Unit 34 — Crime
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 34. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.

items.example: The police are investigating a serious crime.
items.note: The general noun for an offence. Criminal is a person who commits a crime or, as an adjective, relates to crime.

items.example: The police are looking for the criminal.
items.note: An umbrella term for an offender. Robber, burglar and shoplifter refer to more specific offences.

items.example: There was a robbery at the bank last night.
items.note: Robbery is the crime; robber is the person. The verb rob normally takes a person or place as its object.

items.pt: assaltante; ladrão que rouba pessoas ou lugares
items.example: The robber ran away after the attack.
items.note: A robber commits robbery. Say rob someone or rob a bank, but steal someone's money.

items.pt: assaltar; roubar uma pessoa ou um local
items.example: Someone tried to rob the bank yesterday.
items.note: Rob a person or a place, but steal an object. Compare Somebody robbed me and Somebody stole my bag.

items.pt: assaltou; assaltado (passado e particípio de rob)
items.example: A tourist was robbed near the station.
items.note: Robbed is the past tense and past participle of rob. A person or place can be robbed; belongings are stolen.

items.example: The gang planned to rob a bank.
items.note: The bank is the place targeted by the robbers. Say rob a bank, not steal a bank.

items.example: My neighbour was robbed on the way home.
items.note: The person affected can be the subject of the passive: I was robbed. Do not say I was stolen.

items.example: A man was arrested for murder.
items.note: Murder can be a noun or a verb referring to intentional unlawful killing; context determines the grammatical role.

items.example: The murderer was sent to prison.
items.note: A murderer is someone who has committed murder. Avoid labelling an unconvicted suspect as guilty.

items.example: The detective believes somebody murdered the victim.
items.note: Murder is a transitive verb: murder somebody, without an extra preposition.

items.pt: invasão de imóvel para cometer crime, geralmente furto; arrombamento
items.example: There was a burglary at the shop on Sunday.
items.note: Burglary involves entering a building unlawfully to commit a crime, commonly theft; it is not the same offence as robbery.

items.example: A burglar broke into our neighbour’s flat.
items.note: A burglar enters a building unlawfully with criminal intent; a burglar may break into a house or flat.

items.example: Someone tried to break into the house.
items.note: Break into is a phrasal verb meaning enter unlawfully or by force. Forms: break, broke, broken.

items.example: A burglar broke into the empty flat.
items.note: Broke is the past simple of break. The past participle is broken: someone has broken into the flat.

items.pt: assalto a pessoa em lugar público
items.example: The area has had several muggings this year.
items.note: The source describes mugging as attacking someone in a public place and stealing their money.

items.example: The mugger escaped before the police arrived.
items.note: A mugger is a person who mugs somebody, commonly in a public place.

items.example: Two people tried to mug him outside the station.
items.note: Mug takes a person as its object: mug somebody, not mug from somebody.

items.pt: furto de carro; roubo de carro
items.example: Car theft is a problem in that neighbourhood.
items.note: Car theft means stealing a vehicle. Theft concerns the property taken; a thief is the person responsible.

items.example: The police caught a car thief near the supermarket.
items.note: A car thief steals cars. The irregular plural of thief is thieves /θiːvz/.

items.example: A thief took my bicycle from the garden.
items.note: A thief steals something. The plural is thieves, with a change from /f/ to /v/.

items.example: The shop reported a theft to the police.
items.note: The general noun theft is also found in the compound car theft. It refers to stealing property.

items.example: It is wrong to steal another person’s phone.
items.note: Steal normally takes the object taken: steal a bag or steal a car, not rob a bag or rob a car.

items.example: Somebody stole my bike during the night.
items.note: Stole is the past simple of steal; the past participle is stolen.

items.example: My passport has been stolen.
items.note: Stolen is the past participle of steal: My passport has been stolen.

items.example: The police stopped someone trying to steal a car.
items.note: Use steal with the vehicle as object; the source contrasts this pattern with rob somebody or a place.

items.example: The police are investigating drug dealing in the area.
items.note: Drug dealing means illegal trade in drugs; the person involved is a drug dealer.

items.example: The drug dealer was arrested near the station.
items.note: Drug dealer names a person involved in selling illegal drugs. Compare drug dealing for the activity.

items.example: The police found evidence that the group sold drugs.
items.note: Sell – sold – sold is irregular. Drug dealing is explained with sell drugs in the source.

items.example: They sold the car last week.
items.note: Sold is both the past simple and past participle of sell.

items.example: The organisation warned people about illegal drugs.
items.note: Here drugs means illegal drugs. In other contexts, a drug can also be a medicine.

items.example: The article discussed the effects of terrorism.
items.note: Terrorism is the noun for the activity; terrorist is the corresponding person noun.

items.example: The police arrested a suspected terrorist.
items.note: The source groups terrorist with attacks on people or places. Suspected terrorist is preferable before a finding of guilt.

items.example: The group threatened to attack the station.
items.note: Attack is transitive in this sense: attack someone or attack a place, without a following to.

items.example: She was arrested for shoplifting.
items.note: Shoplifting means stealing goods from a shop. It is a noun; the related person is a shoplifter.

items.example: A shoplifter was caught taking some clothes.
items.note: A shoplifter steals items from shops. This differs from a shop assistant, who works there.

items.example: Somebody tried to steal from the local shop.
items.note: Shoplifting is described in the textbook as stealing things from a shop.

items.example: There have been a lot of muggings near the park.
items.note: Mugging can be countable: a mugging, several muggings, a lot of muggings.

items.example: Everyone must obey the law.
items.note: The law refers to legal rules; a court is where legal cases may be heard.

items.example: The officers may arrest the suspect.
items.note: Arrest is transitive: arrest somebody. Being arrested does not, by itself, prove guilt.

items.example: A woman was arrested for shoplifting yesterday.
items.note: Be arrested for + offence is a common pattern; being arrested is not equivalent to being convicted.

items.example: The police are asking witnesses for help.
items.note: In British English, the police normally takes a plural verb: the police are, not the police is.

items.example: A police officer spoke to the shop manager.
items.note: The term police officer appears in exercise 34.2. It refers to one person, unlike the collective the police.

items.example: The case will be heard in court next month.
items.note: Court refers to a place or institution for legal proceedings. Use in court and go to court in judicial contexts.

items.pt: comparecer à Justiça; ir a tribunal
items.example: He has to go to court next Tuesday.
items.note: Go to court usually has no article when referring to legal proceedings.

items.example: The judge found the man guilty.
items.note: Guilty is the opposite of innocent. An accusation or arrest alone does not establish guilt.

items.example: The woman was innocent and went home.
items.note: Innocent is the opposite of guilty. The source contrasts outcomes after going to court.

items.example: He received a fine for parking in the wrong place.
items.note: As a noun, a fine is a monetary penalty. Fine also has a different meaning as an adjective.

items.example: He had to pay a fine for dangerous parking.
items.note: Pay a fine is a fixed collocation. In the exercise, an example concerns a parking offence.

items.example: Her brother works at a prison.
items.note: Prison is a place where people may be held under sentence. Compare in prison with work at a prison.

items.pt: ir para a prisão; ser encarcerado
items.example: The criminal may go to prison for many years.
items.note: Go to prison has no article when describing imprisonment as a punishment.

items.example: The man has been in prison for three years.
items.note: Be in prison describes imprisonment; exercise 34.2 uses a duration with for + period of time.

items.pt: vândalo; pessoa que destrói ou danifica bens
items.example: Some vandals damaged the bus stop.
items.note: A vandal damages or destroys property; vandalism is the related activity noun.

items.example: Vandalism is a problem in the town centre.
items.note: Vandalism refers to deliberate damage to property, such as smashed public facilities.

items.example: Someone tried to break a window at the school.
items.note: Break – broke – broken is irregular. The source illustrates broken windows caused by vandals.

items.example: The vandals tried to smash the streetlights.
items.note: Smash suggests breaking something with force. Compare smash a window with break a window.

items.example: The old telephone box was damaged last week.
items.note: Telephone box is a British English term for a public telephone kiosk, mentioned in the vandalism example.

items.example: Some young people are warned not to take drugs.
items.note: In the source take drugs means use drugs, not transport them. The wider phrase may also mean take medicine in other contexts.

items.pt: violência e desordem de torcidas de futebol
items.example: The report describes ways to reduce football hooliganism.
items.note: Football hooliganism describes violence or serious disorder connected with football supporters or events.

items.example: The police removed a football hooligan from the stadium.
items.note: A football hooligan is a supporter who behaves violently or causes serious trouble, not every football fan.

items.example: There is a football match on Sunday afternoon.
items.note: The source mentions going to a football match in its description of a hooligan.

items.example: A few people came to the event just to make trouble.
items.note: Make trouble is the natural collocation here, not do trouble.

items.example: The children did not mean to damage the trees.
items.note: Damage is a verb taking a direct object, as in damage trees. It appears in an open-ended exercise scenario.

learningObjectives: Match crimes with the people who commit them and the verbs used: robbery/robber/rob, burglary/burglar/break into, shoplifting/shoplifter and others.
Distinguish rob somebody or a place from steal something and form natural passive expressions such as be robbed and be stolen.
Recognise irregular verb forms in context: break–broke–broken, steal–stole–stolen and sell–sold–sold.
Understand and use introductory legal vocabulary: be arrested for, the police, go to court, guilty, innocent, pay a fine and go to prison.
Describe vandalism, illegal drug use and football hooliganism with accurate vocabulary and basic collocations.
Distinguish arrest from proof of guilt and express simple opinions about the possible consequences of offences.
